unit.title: Participate in online networks and social media

summary: This unit teaches you to take part in online networks and social media safely, politely and professionally. You will learn the main kinds of online network, how to set up and protect a profile and an account, how to post, share and reply with good manners, how to follow your workplace's social media rules, and how to deal with scams, false stories and online bullying.

blocks.p: Online networks are part of working life. Customers find a fabrication shop or a villa through its page; supervisors send the day's jobs in a group chat; employers look at applicants' profiles; and one careless post can lose a customer, break a guest's privacy or cost a worker a job. This unit teaches you to use **online networks and social media** in a way that helps your work and your name, and protects you, your employer and the people you serve.

**Who it is for:** this is a general unit in several Level 2 programmes, including Welding and Hospitality (villa and property services), so the examples come from workshops, building sites and villas. The skills are the same on any site or app: this kit describes the kinds of network, not particular brands.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Know the kinds of online network
Tell social networking sites, messaging apps, professional networks, video and photo sites, forums and review sites apart, and say how each is used at work.
Set up a profile
Make a safe, professional profile, leaving out private details and setting who can see what.
Protect your accounts
Use strong, separate passwords and two-step verification, log out of shared computers, and know what to do if an account is hacked.
Spot scams and false information
Recognise phishing links, fake accounts, prize and job scams, and check a story before you share it.
Use good online manners
Post, message and reply politely and clearly, in work groups and in public.
Follow your workplace's rules
Keep customers', guests' and business information private; know who speaks for the business; keep personal and work use apart.
Help a business online
Prepare suitable posts with photos, captions and hashtags, and answer comments and reviews properly.
Deal with bullying and abuse
Do not join in; save evidence, block and report; support the person; get help.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on kinds of network, profiles, privacy, security, scams, netiquette, workplace rules, your digital footprint, copyright, false information, cyberbullying and business use.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as tag, phishing, meme, viral, netiquette, username, DM, feed, troll, cookies, caption) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: planning and preparing professional posts for a small business page, and securing an account and role-playing replies to comments, messages and scams. You use only the Centre's practice account, never your own, and never show a real password.

blocks.note: Many short answers ask for exact words, and several look alike: a **tag** links a person to a post, a **hashtag** groups posts on a topic, and a **caption** is the text under a photo. Learn the key terms in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Online networks and how they work

blocks.p: An **online network** is a group of people who link up and share with each other over the internet. **Social media** are the sites and apps that let them post, share, comment and message.

head: Kind of network
What it is
How it can be used at work
rows: Social networking site
Members make a profile, post photos, videos and messages, and follow or befriend others
A fabrication shop's page showing finished gates and grills; a villa's page showing its rooms and view
Messaging app and group chat
Private messages between people, and groups for a team
The day's job list sent to welders on site; housekeeping saying which rooms are ready
Professional networking site
Profiles that show work history, skills and certificates
Finding a job, linking with employers, showing your NCTVET certificates; employers finding staff
Video-sharing site
Members post and watch videos
Short videos of work being done safely; how-to videos for customers
Photo-sharing site
Mainly photos and short videos, often with hashtags
Before-and-after photos of a job or a room
Online forum or community
People post questions and replies on one topic
Trade questions and answers; supplier and tool advice
Review site
Customers rate and describe businesses
Villas and contractors are judged by their reviews and replies
Video call or online meeting
People see and hear each other live through their cameras
Training sessions; meetings with a supervisor or customer far away

blocks.note: Advice from strangers in a forum or a video can be wrong or unsafe. Never try an electrical, welding, gas or chemical method you saw online without checking it with your instructor or supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Term
What it means
rows: Profile
The page that shows others who you are: name, photo, short description and posts
Username (handle)
The name you sign in with or are known by, often shown with @ in front
Post
Something you put online: words, a photo, a video or a link
Feed (timeline)
The list of new posts from people and pages you follow, which you scroll through
Story
A post that disappears from view after a set time (often 24 hours) on many sites
Comment
A reply written under a post, which others can usually see
Like (reaction)
A small sign, such as a thumbs-up or heart, clicked to show you enjoy a post
Share (repost)
Passing someone's post on to your own contacts
Tag
Adding a person's name to a photo or post, so that it links to their account
Mention
Writing @ and a username in a post, so that person is told about it
Hashtag
A word or phrase after #, such as #SteelGates, that groups posts on one topic so people can find them
DM
Direct message: a private message to one person or a small group
Caption
The short text under a photo that explains it
Followers, friends, connections
The people who see your posts and whose posts you see
Page and group
A page is a public presence for a business; a group is a place for members to talk together
Meme
A funny picture or short video idea that is copied and shared widely
Viral
A post that has been shared so much that huge numbers of people see it quickly has "gone viral"
Sponsored post (advert)
A post a business pays the site to show to many people
Cookies
Small files a website stores on your device to remember you; they can be cleared in the browser settings

blocks.h: How feeds choose what you see

blocks.p: Most sites use a computer program (an **algorithm**) to choose which posts appear in your feed, mostly ones like those you have liked, watched or commented on before. This keeps you scrolling, and it means you mainly see one side of a story. It also means a post that people react to angrily can spread further than a calm, true one.

sections.title: Setting up a safe, professional profile

flow: Read the site's rules and privacy terms, so you know how it uses your information (most sites need you to be at least 13)
Sign up with an email address you check often, and a sensible username
Set a strong password that you use nowhere else, and turn on two-step verification
Add a clear, friendly photo of your face and an honest, short description of your trade and skills
Leave out private details (see the table below)
Open the privacy settings: choose who can see your posts, friends list and contact details; turn off location sharing; review tags before they appear
View your profile as the public sees it, and fix anything that does not look professional

head: Put on a work profile
Keep off any public profile
rows: Your name as it appears on your certificates
Your home address and the times your home is empty
Your trade and level, for example "Level 2 welding trainee" or "Villa housekeeping attendant"
Your date of birth
The parish or town where you work
Your TRN, passport number or other ID numbers
Skills, certificates (NCTVET, HEART/NSTA Trust) and work experience
Bank or card details, passwords and PINs
A clear, friendly photo of your face
Your phone number, unless it is a work number you want customers to use
Photos of your own finished work, with permission
Photos of your children, or of other people without their permission

ul: A username such as **@shericka_morgan** or your full name is right for a work profile; a nickname or a joke name is not.
A profile photo should show your face clearly, in good light, dressed as you would be for work. Party photos, cartoons and football badges belong elsewhere.
Keep a professional profile up to date: add each new certificate and job.
A professional networking profile can also show recommendations from supervisors and instructors. Ask them first.

head: Audience
Who can see it
rows: Public
**Anyone** on the internet, including strangers, employers and criminals, and search engines may show it
Friends, followers or connections
Only people you have accepted, and sometimes their friends when you are tagged
Custom or close friends
Only the people you choose
Only me
Only you

ul: Check the audience every time you post, especially on a new site or after an app update.
Turn off **location sharing** on posts and photos. A photo can show strangers where you live, where you are now, or that you are far from home.
Never post that your home will be empty ("Off to Miami for two weeks!"). Share holiday photos after you get back.
Turn on the setting that lets you review tags before they appear on your profile.

blocks.p: Your **digital footprint** is the trail of everything you have posted, shared, liked and commented on, and what others have posted about you. It lasts. Deleting a post removes it from your page, but others may already have **saved, copied or screenshotted** it. Employers, customers and schools often look people up online before they hire or deal with them.

blocks.note: Before you post, ask: **would I be happy for my supervisor, a customer and my family to see this, today and in five years' time?** If the answer is no, do not post it.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Protection
What to do
rows: Strong passwords
Long and hard to guess: a passphrase of several words with numbers and symbols mixed in. Never your name, birthday or 12345678.
A different password for every account
If one site is broken into and your password stolen, criminals try it on all your other accounts. Different passwords keep them safe.
Two-step verification
A code sent to your phone (or made by an app) is needed as well as the password, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
Never share your password
Not with a friend, a co-worker or anyone who "needs to post something for their business". They can open their own account.
Shared computers
On a Centre, library or office computer, log out when you finish and do not let the browser save your password. A private (incognito) window helps, but still log out.
Updates
Install app and system updates when offered: many fix security holes.
Recovery details
Keep the account's recovery email and phone number up to date, so you can get back in if you are locked out.
Third-party apps and quizzes
Games and quizzes ("Which fruit are you?") that ask to connect to your account may collect your details and your friends'. Do not give them access.
Log-in alerts
Turn on alerts for log-ins from new devices, and check the list of devices logged in to your account from time to time.

blocks.h: Signs that an account has been hacked

ul: Posts or messages you did not write, often adverts or strange links sent to your friends.
Your password suddenly does not work, or the email or phone number on the account has changed.
Alerts about log-ins from places or devices you do not know.
Friends asking why you sent them a message.

flow: If you can still log in, change the password at once (on a device you trust)
In the security settings, log out of all other devices and turn on two-step verification
Check that the recovery email and phone number are still yours
If you cannot log in, use the site's account-recovery or "hacked account" help pages
Warn your friends and contacts not to trust or click anything the account sent
Delete posts and messages the hacker sent; if it is a work account, tell your supervisor straight away
Change the password on any other account that used the same password

sections.title: Scams, fake accounts and false information

head: Scam
What it looks like
What to do
rows: Phishing link
A message from a "friend" or a "company": "Is this you in this video?", "Your account will be closed", with a link to a page that asks you to log in
Do not click. Check with the friend another way. Log in only by opening the app or typing the address yourself.
Fake prize or giveaway
"You have won a phone! Pay delivery to claim it", or a copy of a real business's page offering prizes
Never pay to receive a prize. Report the account.
Impersonation
A new account using a real person's name and photo (a friend, a pastor, a supervisor) asking for money, phone credit or gift cards
Check with the real person by phone or face to face. Report the fake account.
Job scam
An offer of an overseas or hotel job if you pay a fee for a "visa", "medical" or "processing"
Check with the real employer or the official programme. Do not pay strangers.
Marketplace scam
Goods at a very low price, with a deposit to be paid before you see them
Meet in a safe public place; see the goods before paying; be wary of prices far too low.
Romance or friendship scam
A new online "friend" who quickly asks for money for an emergency
Do not send money to people you have not met. Talk to someone you trust.

ul: It is **too good to be true**: a prize you did not enter, a well-paid job with no interview, goods for almost nothing.
It **hurries** you: "today only", "your account closes in 24 hours".
It asks for **money, passwords, codes or bank details**, or a fee before you get something.
The account is **new**, with few friends or posts, even if it uses a real person's photo.
Spelling mistakes, strange links, and a request to move to a private chat or another app.

blocks.note: Real overseas work programmes, such as the farm and hotel work programmes run through the Ministry of Labour and Social Security, are not arranged by strangers in a DM who ask for money. Check any job offer with the official body, and be very wary of anyone asking you to pay to secure a place.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: False stories, edited photos and rumours spread fast, especially forwarded voice notes and messages "from a friend who works there". Some are mistakes; some are made up on purpose. Sharing them can frighten people, make them act wrongly (stockpiling, moving guests, missing work), damage a person's or a business's name, and make you look careless.

flow: Stop: do not share straight away, even if it says "share now"
Who posted it? A known news service, a government body or the company itself, or an unknown account or a forwarded message with no name?
Read the whole story, not just the headline, and check the date: old stories are often shared again
Look for warning signs: a shocking headline in capitals, many spelling mistakes, no names or places
Check whether trusted news services or the official body are saying the same thing
For a photo, do a picture search to see if it is old or from somewhere else
If you still cannot be sure, do not share it; for work matters, ask your supervisor

blocks.note: For storms, earthquakes and floods, rely on official sources such as the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) and the Meteorological Service, and for water or power lock-offs, the utility's own official notices. A voice note from "a cousin who works there" is not an official source.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Clickbait** is a headline made to trick you into clicking ("You won't believe what this welder found!"). It is often harmless but wastes time, and some clickbait leads to scam pages or malware.

blocks.note: If you find you have shared something false, delete it and post a short correction. Owning a mistake protects your name far more than leaving it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Netiquette** means the good manners people expect online. Online, people cannot see your face or hear your voice, so words are easily misread, and what you write can be copied and kept for ever.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Think before you post: would you say it to the person's face, in front of your supervisor?
Post when you are angry. Calm down first, and talk to the person directly.
Be polite and respectful, even when you disagree
Insult, threaten, mock or swear at anyone
Write work messages clearly, in full words, with correct spelling
Type in ALL CAPITALS: it reads as shouting
Ask before you post or share someone's photo, or tag them
Share other people's photos, numbers or private stories without permission
Keep work groups to work topics
Send chain messages, jokes that may offend, or adverts for your side business in a work group
Message co-workers at sensible times
Message late at night unless it is urgent
Reply in good time, and say when you will answer fully
Leave work messages unanswered for days
Check facts before you share
Forward rumours
Delete and say sorry if you post in the wrong place
Leave it, or bury it under more messages

ul: Start with a greeting and put the key facts first: who, what, where, when. For example: "Good morning. Villa 3 guests have asked for late checkout at 2 p.m. Please clean Villa 3 last."
Reply to the group only when everyone needs the answer; reply privately for the rest.
Use @mentions to show who a message is for.
Keep voice notes short, and type anything people must refer back to, such as times, sizes and addresses.
Use emojis sparingly in work messages: they can be misread or look unprofessional.
If a discussion turns into an argument, stop typing and talk to the person directly, or ask the supervisor.
Join on time, from a quiet place, with your full name showing.
Mute your microphone when you are not speaking: workshop noise, traffic and chatter spoil the call for everyone.
Turn the camera on if asked; check what is behind you before you do.
Raise your hand or wait for a pause before speaking, and keep to the topic.

sections.title: Social media at work: rules, privacy and your reputation

blocks.p: Many employers have a **social media policy**: the rules on how staff use social media about work. It protects the business's good name, its customers and guests, and its staff. Read it, and ask if you are not sure.

head: A policy usually says
For example
rows: Do not share private business information
Prices the business keeps private, plans, alarm codes, keys, staff rosters, security arrangements
Do not post customers, guests or their property without permission
No photos of a customer's house, car or family; no word about who is staying at a villa
Only named people speak for the business
Only the manager or the person given the job answers questions and reviews on the official page
Be respectful about the employer, co-workers, customers and other businesses
No complaints about the boss or a customer in public posts; no jokes about rival firms
Bullying online is dealt with like bullying at work
Mocking a co-worker in a group chat is treated as a discipline matter
When phones may be used at work
On breaks only; never near running machines or hot work
What happens if the rules are broken
Warnings, discipline, or dismissal for serious breaches

blocks.h: Privacy of customers, guests and co-workers

ul: A guest's stay, a customer's address, the work done in their home and what they paid are **private**. Never post them, even "nicely", and even after the guest has left.
Never post photos of documents (passports, ID cards, invoices), alarm panels, keys or safes.
Ask a co-worker before posting a photo of them. A "funny" photo of someone asleep on a break, or making a mistake, can humiliate them and is a form of bullying.
Do not post photos or details of accidents or injuries at work: report them through the proper channel.
Jamaica's data protection law expects businesses to keep personal information about customers and guests safe. As a worker, you help by keeping it off social media.

blocks.p: Keep your **personal** account for your own life and the **work** account (if you are given one) for the business. This keeps private life apart from work, stops personal posts appearing to come from the business, and means the business keeps its page if you leave. Do not use the business page to argue or for your own opinions.

Checking social media during work takes attention off the job. In a workshop that can be dangerous: a grinder operator or welder who looks at a phone can lose focus, and someone walking while scrolling can trip over cables or walk into a work area without PPE. In a villa, a housekeeper on the phone may leave a room half done or seem rude to guests. Use your phone for personal things on your break, or in an emergency, as your employer's rules allow.

ul: Photos, videos, music, logos and writing found online belong to the person or business that made them. You need **permission or the right to use them** before using them in a post or advert, even with a credit.
Use your own photos of your own work, photos the business owns, or ones offered for free use under their stated terms.
Never pass off someone else's work (another shop's gate, another villa's pool) as yours.

blocks.h: Posts that help or harm your future

head: Helps your name
Harms your chances
rows: Photos of your certificate or awards day at the Centre
Rude jokes or complaints about a past boss, co-workers or customers
Your own finished project, posted with permission
Photos of fights, heavy drinking or illegal activity
Thanking instructors and supervisors
Insults, threats or bullying
Sharing useful, true trade information
Sharing false stories and rumours

blocks.note: Jamaica's cybercrimes law makes it an offence to get into someone else's account without permission, and to use a computer to send threatening or menacing messages. What you post can have legal consequences, not only social ones.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Using social media for a business

blocks.p: A small business, such as a welding shop, an electrical contractor or a villa, can use social media cheaply to show its work and win customers, if it is done well and honestly.

head: Step
What to do
rows: Set up an official page
Business name and logo, area served, opening hours, a phone number and how to send a message
Agree the page's rules
What may be posted, what must never be posted, and who answers the public
Post real work regularly
Clear photos and short videos of finished gates, railings, wiring jobs, rooms and the view; before-and-after; a short, useful tip
Write good captions
Short, plain and polite; what the job is and the area (not the address); how to get in touch
Use a few suitable hashtags
Two or three that describe the work and area, such as #SteelGates #StCatherine, not long lists of unrelated popular tags
Answer messages and comments quickly
A fast, polite reply often turns into a sale; pass questions on prices and bookings to the person responsible
Share reviews and offers
With the customer's permission; offers for slow seasons, with honest conditions
Watch what works
Which posts bring likes, shares, messages and real enquiries, and post more like them

ul: Get the **customer's permission**, and the employer's, before posting photos of work at a customer's home or business.
Leave out anything that shows **where the customer lives**: house numbers, street signs, licence plates, the view from the gate. Crop, blur or take the photo again. Turn off location tagging.
Leave out people (unless they agree), valuables and security features.
Clear away tools, offcuts and rubbish, and take clear, well-lit photos of neat, finished work.
In workshop photos, everyone must be wearing the right **PPE** and working safely. A photo of a welder with no helmet or gloves tells customers the business is careless, and sets a bad example.

head: What comes in
A good response
rows: A kind review
Thank the customer politely by name and invite them back. Keep it short.
A complaint or bad review
The person responsible replies, promptly (within a day if possible), calmly and politely
Thank them for the feedback and say sorry the job or stay was not what they expected; no arguing and no blaming anyone by name
Leave out private details: no address, room number, invoice or booking details
Say briefly what is being done, and invite them to message or call so it can be sorted out privately
Then really fix the problem
A question about prices or bookings
Reply politely and invite them to message or call the person who handles prices and bookings
A rude or insulting comment
Do not argue in public. The person responsible may reply once, calmly, or hide or report it under the site's rules
Spam or a scam link in the comments
Delete or hide it and report the account

blocks.note: People reading a review judge the business more by the **reply** than by the complaint. A calm, helpful reply can win back the customer and show future customers that the business cares; an angry one can go viral for the wrong reasons.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Photos, prices and offers must be true and up to date. Show your own work, not photos from elsewhere. Say whether prices include GCT, and keep offers to their stated terms. False adverts lose trust fast, and customers will say so in public.

sections.title: Cyberbullying, trolls and staying well online

blocks.p: **Cyberbullying** is using the internet or phones to hurt, frighten, embarrass or shut someone out, again and again: nasty messages, threats, spreading rumours, posting embarrassing photos, fake accounts that mock a person, or leaving someone out of a group on purpose. A **troll** is a person who posts insulting comments on purpose to start arguments.

flow: Do not reply or hit back: that is what the bully or troll wants, and it can make you look like the one at fault
Save the evidence: screenshots showing the messages, the account name and the date
Block the account, and report it to the site using its report tools
Tell someone you trust: your supervisor, instructor or a family member
If there are threats of harm, threats to share private images, or you feel unsafe, report it to the police

blocks.h: If it happens to someone else

ul: Do not join in, like it, or share it, even as a joke.
Support the person privately: tell them it is not their fault and help them save the evidence.
Report it to the site, and to a supervisor if it is in a work group or about a co-worker.
Never repost bullying to "expose" it: that spreads it further.
Turn off notifications you do not need, and keep the phone away at meals, at work and at bedtime.
Unfollow or mute accounts that make you angry or anxious.
Remember that most people post only their best moments. Do not judge your life by other people's feeds.
Take a break from social media if it is upsetting you, and talk to someone.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and talk it through with your instructor.

ul: I can name the main kinds of online network and say how each can be used at work.
I can explain profile, username, feed, post, story, tag, mention, hashtag, DM, caption, meme, viral and cookies.
I can set up a safe, professional profile and choose what to leave off it.
I can set privacy settings, turn off location sharing and check who can see my posts.
I can explain what a digital footprint is and why employers look at it.
I can protect an account with a strong, separate password and two-step verification, and log out of shared computers.
I can spot the signs of a hacked account and say what to do.
I can recognise phishing links, fake prizes, fake accounts and job scams.
I can check whether a story is true before I share it.
I can follow the rules of netiquette in posts, group chats and online meetings.
I can explain what a workplace social media policy covers and follow it.
I can keep customers', guests' and co-workers' information private.
I can explain copyright and why I need permission to use other people's photos and music.
I can prepare a suitable post for a business page, with a good photo, caption and hashtags.
I can say how a business should answer good and bad reviews.
I can deal with cyberbullying and trolls, and help someone who is being bullied.

terms: The computer program that chooses which posts appear in your feed
The short text under a photo that explains it
A headline made to trick you into clicking
Small files a website stores on your device to remember you
Using the internet or phones to hurt, frighten or embarrass someone
The lasting trail of what you have posted and done online
The list of new posts you scroll through; also called the timeline
A word or phrase after #, used to group posts on a topic
A fake account pretending to be a real person or business
A sign such as a thumbs-up or heart, clicked to show you enjoy a post; also called a reaction
A funny picture or short video idea copied and shared widely
People who link up and share with each other online
A fake message that tries to trick you into giving a password or bank details
Settings that control who can see your posts and details
The page that shows others who you are
A saved picture of what is on your screen
A workplace's rules on how staff use social media about work
A post a business pays the site to show widely; an advert
Adding a person's name to a photo or post so that it links to their account
A person who posts insulting comments on purpose to start arguments
A log-in that needs a code as well as the password; also called two-factor
The name you sign in with, often shown with @; also called a handle
A live online meeting where people see and hear each other
Shared so widely and quickly that huge numbers of people see it

c1.title: A business page for a grill shop in Linstead
c1.text: Mr Barrett runs a small gate and grill shop in Linstead, St Catherine. He asks Akeem, a trainee on work experience, to help start a page for the business. Mr Barrett will answer all questions about prices himself. Akeem has three photos to choose from: a new grill at a customer's house, with the house number and the family car's licence plate in the shot; a welder in the workshop working without a helmet or gloves; and a neat close-up of a finished gate in the yard.

c2.title: Job hunting from St Ann's Bay
c2.text: Shericka has just finished her Level 2 at a HEART/NSTA Trust centre and is applying for jobs with a villa company near St Ann's Bay. She is setting up a profile on a professional networking site. Her personal social media username is @ShekaPartyQueen, her posts are public, and two years ago she posted an angry rant naming a supervisor at her last job.

c3.title: A hacked account and a fake supervisor in Bog Walk
c3.text: Devon is an apprentice with an electrical contractor in Bog Walk, St Catherine. His friends tell him that his social media account has been posting adverts for cheap phones with a strange link. He can still log in. The same week, several workers at the firm get a friend request from an account with the supervisor's name and photo, opened a few days earlier and with almost no friends, asking them to buy phone credit and send the codes urgently.

c4.title: A rumour in a villa staff group in Runaway Bay
c4.text: Monique works at a villa company in Runaway Bay, St Ann. In the staff group chat, someone forwards a voice note: "From a cousin who works at the water company: water will be off in the whole area for five days from tomorrow. Move all the guests!" Later, a co-worker posts a photo of a guest's passport left in a room, asking, "Whose is this?"

c5.title: Reviews for an electrical contractor in Lucea
c5.text: Sheldon works for an electrical contractor in Lucea, Hanover. The firm's office manager answers its page. A customer, Mrs Wright, posts a one-star review: "They rewired my shop and left dust everywhere, and now the lights flicker." It is 10 p.m. when Sheldon sees it, and he is angry, because he worked on that job and thinks the customer is being unfair.

questions.q: What should Akeem do with the photo of the grill at the customer's house?
o: Post it as it is, because the grill is the best one the shop has made
Post it, but only after the customer has paid for the work in full
Ask the customer first, and crop out the number and plate
Post it on his own page first, to see whether people like it
questions.why: The customer must agree before their home is shown, and the house number and licence plate would tell strangers where the family lives. Crop or blur them, or retake the photo, and turn off location.

questions.q: Why should the workshop photo not be posted?
o: It shows unsafe work and sets a bad example
Workshop photos are never allowed on a business page
The welder may want to be paid for being in the photo
It will use too much of the shop's mobile data to post
questions.why: A welder without a helmet or gloves shows customers a business that ignores safety. Photos for a page must show work being done the right way, with the right PPE, and with the person's permission.

questions.q: Which set of hashtags is best for the gate photo?
o: #love #goodvibes #photooftheday #happy #fun
#SteelGates #Linstead #StCatherine
#BestGatesInTheWorldNoCompetition
#gate #gate #gate #gate #gate #gate
questions.why: A few hashtags that describe the work and the area help local customers find the post. Long lists of unrelated popular tags, or repeated tags, look like spam and bring the wrong viewers.

questions.q: A customer asks in a public comment how much a gate like this costs. How should Akeem reply?
o: Guess a price from what he has heard around the workshop
Ignore it, since only Mr Barrett may talk about prices
Post the full price list of the shop under the comment
Thank them and invite them to call Mr Barrett
questions.why: Prices are Mr Barrett's job, but the customer still deserves a quick, polite answer. Pointing them to the right person keeps the enquiry alive and avoids a wrong price in public.

questions.q: Which username is best for Shericka's professional profile?
o: @ShekaPartyQueen, so friends can find her
@shericka_morgan, her own full name
@VillaQueen2026, to show she wants villa work
@HireMeNow, so employers know she needs work
questions.why: Employers expect a professional profile to carry your real name, matching your certificates and application. A nickname or a slogan looks unprofessional and is harder to find.

questions.q: Which detail should Shericka leave off her profile?
o: Her NCTVET Level 2 certificate
The parish where she wants to work
Her TRN and her date of birth
Her skills in housekeeping
questions.why: A TRN and date of birth help criminals pretend to be you. Certificates, skills and the area you want to work in are exactly what an employer wants to see.

questions.q: What should she do about the old rant naming her former supervisor?
o: Delete it, knowing others may already have copied it
Leave it, since it is two years old and nobody will look
Edit it to remove only the supervisor's surname
Share it again so that it moves to the bottom of her page
questions.why: Employers often look applicants up, and an attack on a past supervisor is a warning sign to them. Deleting it helps, but it may already have been screenshotted, which is why it is best never to post in anger.

questions.q: Devon can still log in. What should he do first?
o: Delete the account and open a new one with a new name
Wait a few days to see whether the adverts stop by themselves
Change the password, log out other devices, and turn on two-step
Post a public message asking the hacker to stop using his account
questions.why: Changing the password and logging out every other device shuts the hacker out; two-step verification stops them getting back in with a stolen password. Then he can clear up the posts and warn friends.

questions.q: Why should Devon also warn his friends and contacts?
o: So that they can report him to the site as a spammer
The hacker may have sent them scam links in his name
So that they all change their own passwords at once
So that the site gives him back his old followers
questions.why: A hacked account is used to send scam links to people who trust the owner. A warning stops friends clicking, and lets them report any messages they got.

questions.q: Which detail best shows the "supervisor" account is fake?
o: It uses the real supervisor's own photo
It is days old, with almost no friends
It sent the request during working hours
It is written in short, simple sentences
questions.why: Fake accounts often copy a real person's photo and name, so the photo proves nothing. A brand-new account with almost no friends, asking for money or credit in a hurry, is the warning sign. Check with the real supervisor in person and report the account.

questions.q: What should Monique do about the voice note?
o: Forward it to her family so that they can store water
Start moving the guests' bags to be ready for tomorrow
Check official notices and ask the supervisor
Reply in the group that it is definitely a lie
questions.why: A forwarded voice note is a rumour until an official source confirms it. Check the water company's own notices and ask the supervisor, and do not forward or act on it until then.

questions.q: The voice note says it came from "a cousin who works at the water company". Why is that not enough?
o: Water company staff are not allowed to use voice notes
Voice notes are always false, whoever sends them
The cousin may not live in the Runaway Bay area
Nobody can check who the cousin is or what they said
questions.why: A claim from an unnamed person cannot be checked, and forwarded messages change as they pass along. Real lock-off notices come from the utility's official channels.

questions.q: What is the right response to the passport photo?
o: Ask for it to be deleted, and tell the supervisor
Reply with the guest's name so that the owner is found quickly
Leave it, since the group is only for the villa's own staff
Save a copy of the photo in case the guest asks later
questions.why: A passport holds a guest's private details, and a group photo can be saved and shared beyond the staff. Delete it, and let the supervisor return the passport through the proper channel.

questions.q: Which reply from the office manager is best?
o: "Our team left your shop spotless. The flickering is caused by your old fittings."
"Thank you, and we're sorry. Please message us so we can visit and put it right."
"We are very disappointed that you posted this instead of calling us first."
"Please remove this review now. We will only discuss the job when you do."
questions.why: A calm reply that thanks, apologises and moves the matter to a private message shows other readers that the firm cares. Arguing, blaming or demanding removal in public makes the firm look worse.

questions.q: What must the public reply leave out?
o: Any thanks to the customer for their feedback
A short apology for the trouble caused
An offer to come back and check the lights
The customer's address and what the job cost
questions.why: The address and the price are the customer's private information. Thanks, an apology and an offer to fix the problem all belong in a good reply.

questions.q: What should Sheldon do about the review tonight?
o: Leave it to the manager, and brief her tomorrow
Reply from his own account to defend the team while it is fresh
Message the customer privately to explain that she is wrong
Ask his friends to post good reviews to push hers down
questions.why: Only the person the firm has chosen answers for it, and replying in anger at night rarely ends well. Sheldon's facts about the job are useful: he should give them to the manager calmly.

questions.q: Kadeem wants to post a photo of his new work ID card as a story, because "stories disappear after a day". Why is that unwise?
o: Stories are only seen by people who already follow him
Viewers can screenshot or save a story before it goes
Stories make the photo look blurred and hard to read
Stories are always shown to his employer before posting
questions.why: A story disappears from view, but anyone who sees it can capture it, and an ID card holds details criminals can use. Never post ID cards, passes or documents.

questions.q: Tishana joins an online training session from a busy workshop. What should she do when she is not speaking?
o: Turn her camera off and leave the meeting running
Keep her microphone on so she can answer quickly
Mute her microphone until she needs to speak
Turn the speaker volume right down so she hears less
questions.why: Grinders, hammers and talk from an open microphone drown out the speaker for everyone. Mute when listening and unmute to speak; better still, move somewhere quieter.

questions.q: A quiz app asks to connect to your account and read your profile and friends list before it will show "which Jamaican parish matches your personality". What should you do?
o: Allow it, since quizzes are only for fun
Allow it, then remove it next week
Allow it if several friends have done it
Refuse, as it would collect your data
questions.why: Quiz apps that ask for account access may collect your details and your friends' details, and some are run by scammers. A quiz does not need your friends list.

questions.q: A stranger sends Rushane a DM offering a hotel job in Canada if he pays J$40,000 for "visa processing" to a personal account. What should he do?
o: Pay half now and the rest when the visa arrives
Ask for the stranger's ID, then pay if it looks real
Check with the official programme; pay nothing
Share the offer with friends so they can apply too
questions.why: A fee to a personal account, an offer out of the blue and a rush are classic signs of a job scam. Real overseas work programmes can be checked with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.
